methodology.target: House adoption of at least one article and Senate conviction on at least one article by the stated deadline, including proceedings after departure.
methodology.limits: Subjective political estimates, not calibrated odds or criminal-guilt judgments. Cases are not independent. Watchlist entries have no estimate; they are not zero risk. Close rankings are uncertain.
methodology.arithmetic: Overall conviction equals House impeachment multiplied by conviction conditional on impeachment. Probabilities across people do not sum to 100%.
methodology.momentum_rule: Assess changes in the political cost and feasibility of later proceedings, including unrelated cases. Record normalization, exceptional-case and backlash explanations; update every affected case with evidence or an explicit hold. Never apply a fixed uplift or infer guilt from another official’s conviction.
methodology.departure_rule: Resignation or dismissal does not automatically preclude impeachment or trial. Consider continuing accountability and disqualification incentives, contested jurisdiction and timing of alleged acts.
methodology.cadence: Daily: resolve procedural outcomes and assess material case or momentum developments; append a dated review even on holds. Reassess odds when material evidence warrants, otherwise hold explicitly. Weekly: compare all cases, discover omitted officials, challenge coalitions and momentum pathways, and review dated tests. No separate scheduled job.

history.summary: The House sent the resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to the Judiciary Committee. The estimated chance that the House impeaches him by November 10, 2027 fell from 60% to 50%. If the House impeaches him, his estimated chance of Senate conviction remains 25%. The estimated chance of both outcomes fell from 15% to 12.5%. The other cases retain their previous estimates or remain unestimated.
history.coverage: Focused review of the House roll call, White House position, Republican leadership and Epstein report. The Guilfoyle records deadline and the January congressional agenda remain open. These probabilities are judgments about outcomes by November 10, 2027.

context.assessment: The House referral shows Republican cohesion on one procedural vote in the outgoing Congress. It supplies no direct evidence about a Senate conviction coalition or about how senators would respond to an unrelated case. The incoming House can revisit the issue in January.

pathways.title: A Senate conviction could make it easier to pursue another case
pathways.assessment: If voters and party leaders accept a bipartisan conviction, lawmakers may feel freer to support another case and witnesses may be more willing to come forward.

pathways.title: Senators could limit their support to one unusual case
pathways.assessment: Senators may agree to convict over a particular official’s actions while continuing to defend other officials facing different allegations.

pathways.title: Voter backlash could discourage another impeachment
pathways.assessment: If lawmakers lose backing after supporting a conviction, colleagues may be less willing to vote for another impeachment or conviction.

hegseth.reason: The outgoing House blocked an immediate vote on the articles. A projected Democratic majority gives a new effort a viable route after January, and its agenda is still open. Those competing facts put House impeachment near even odds by November 10, 2027. The referral supplies no direct evidence about whether two-thirds of senators present would convict.

momentum.assessment: Trump’s backing and the referral block the immediate route to adoption. The incoming Democratic House still has a route to take up the allegations. The vote supplies no direct evidence of a Senate conviction coalition.

The White House’s warning about future investigations drew public resistance. The Mississippi Senate call widens the incoming Democratic majority, which still falls short of the votes needed for conviction if all senators are present. All existing estimates through November 10, 2027 are held.

No new case-specific Senate commitments or conviction were verified.
